title: Using AI as a Parent
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing as a self-described AI non-expert, Stuart recounts a specific home moment — helping his eighth-grade daughter with algebra homework — where he turned to ChatGPT and found it genuinely useful, not for the answer itself but for the worked method that let him relearn forgotten math well enough to actually teach her. He's careful to frame the piece narrowly: this is a parent's anecdote about a household use case, not a claim about AI's broader effect on classrooms, teaching, or the future of education, territory he explicitly defers to more expert colleagues. From that single experience he draws two limits on what the tool can do: it can't manufacture the parent's care that made him seek help in the first place, and it can't do the learning for his daughter — only she can do that by engaging with the method rather than skipping to the answer. The piece closes by naming itself as small and personal, "just a blog post by a thankful parent," rather than a broader argument about AI in education.
points: Draws a clear line between AI as a homework tool for a specific home task versus AI as a classroom or pedagogical intervention, explicitly declining to generalize beyond his own family's use case.
Identifies the actual value of the AI interaction as the worked method, not the bare answer — the tool let him relearn forgotten content well enough to teach it himself.
Names two hard limits on what AI can substitute for in a home-learning context: it can't create the parent's motivating care, and it can't do the cognitive work of learning on the student's behalf.
Models a father's own household decision about when and how to use a tech tool with his child, rather than a school-policy or classroom-practice argument.
quotes: As I've said in recent articles, I'm intentionally not good at most things related to teaching. To me, this is the key to being a good teacher while having a life.

Which is all to say, I'm not an expert on AI. It's effects on teaching, how to use it in the classroom, what it's doing to us and our students, where it will take education in the next five years…my answers to these questions are about as authoritative as any random teacher you'd ask.

It didn't just tell me the answer — I had the back of the textbook for that unhelpful bit of info. Instead, it gave me the full method for solving the problem. Once I read it, I knew how to help Haddie.

It can't make us care about others. I had to care about helping my daughter with homework to use the tool. And then I had to care way more to use the tool to help my daughter learn versus just using the tool to skip work.
It can't make us learn. Learning takes work — there's no away around it. You only remember what you think about, and if ChatGPT or its ilk do all the "thinking," well…you won't do the learning.
